items.prose: A research team ran six variants of a carry signal, A to F, each for 9 months, and logged each month's return in %. A one-way ANOVA rejects equal means at 5%, with a within-variant sum of squares of 172.8. The variant means are A 0.3, B 1.4, C 2.2, D 3.8, E 0.9 and F 1.2. The team now asks which pairs of variants differ.

parts.question: What is the within-variant mean square? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: Six variants of 9 months leave $54 - 6 = 48$ degrees of freedom, so $172.8/48 = 3.6$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the within-variant sum by its degrees of freedom, months less variants.

byKey.n-minus-one: 3.2604 is $172.8/53$. Each variant's own mean uses up a degree of freedom, six in all, so divide by 48.
byKey.all-months: 3.2 is $172.8/54$, one per month. The six variant means were estimated from the same months, so 48 remain.

explain.text: The 54 months scatter round six fitted means, which costs 6 degrees of freedom. So the mean square is $172.8/48 = 3.6$, an estimate of the month-to-month variance.

parts.question: Every pair of variants gets its own two-sided test. Bonferroni's correction shares 5% equally among the tests, so the chance of any false difference is at most 5%. What level does each test use? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Six variants make $\binom62 = 15$ pairs, so each test runs at $0.05/15 \approx 0.0033$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the pairs of variants, then share the 5% among them.

byKey.per-variant: 0.0083 is $0.05/6$, one share per variant. The tests are of pairs, and six variants make 15 of them.
byKey.halved: 0.0017 is $0.05/30$. Each two-sided test splits its own level between the tails; the correction shares 0.05 among the 15 tests.

explain.text: Each pair is one test, and six variants give $6 \times 5/2 = 15$ pairs. Bonferroni gives each test $0.05/15$, so the chance that any of them rejects by luck stays at most 5%.

parts.question: Take the mean square 3.6 from part 1. What is the standard error of the gap between two variant means? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Each mean of 9 months has variance $3.6/9 = 0.4$, and two of them add: $\sqrt{0.8} \approx 0.8944$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the variances of the two means, then take the root.

byKey.variance: 0.8 is the variance of the difference, $2 \times 3.6/9$. The standard error is its square root.
byKey.one-mean: 0.6325 is $\sqrt{3.6/9}$, for one variant's mean. A difference of two independent means carries both variances: $\sqrt{0.8}$.

explain.text: The mean square 3.6 estimates the variance of one month's return, whichever variant ran it. A mean of 9 months has variance 0.4, and a difference of two such means has 0.8. Its root is 0.8944.

parts.question: At the level of part 2, a two-sided $t$-test on 48 degrees of freedom rejects beyond 3.0892. Take the standard error 0.8944 from part 3. What is the smallest gap between two variant means that it calls significant? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $3.0892 \times 0.8944 \approx 2.763$: two variant means must sit at least 2.763 apart.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the critical value by the standard error of a difference.

byKey.variance: 2.471 multiplies by the variance 0.8. The critical value counts standard errors, so use $\sqrt{0.8} = 0.8944$.
byKey.one-mean: 1.954 uses the standard error of one mean, 0.6325. The gap is a difference of two means, with standard error 0.8944.
byKey.normal-five: 1.753 is $1.96 \times 0.8944$, a single test at 5%. With 15 tests each runs at 0.0033, so the bar rises to 3.0892 standard errors.

explain.text: A pair differs when its gap passes 3.0892 standard errors. So the bar is $3.0892 \times 0.8944 \approx 2.763$, in % a month. A lone 5% test would need only 1.753.

parts.question: Using the bar 2.763 from part 4, how many of the 15 pairs of variants differ?

feedback.correct: Only D against A (3.5) and D against E (2.9) clear 2.763. D against F, at 2.6, falls just short.
feedback.generic: Not quite. List the gaps between the six means and keep those of 2.763 or more.

byKey.normal-five: 5 counts the gaps above 1.753, the bar for one 5% test. With 15 tests at once that bar lets too many false alarms through; use 2.763.
byKey.one-mean: 4 counts the gaps above 1.954, a bar built on one mean's standard error. On 2.763 only two pairs remain.
byKey.variance: 3 counts the gaps above 2.471, a bar built on the variance. On 2.763, D against F (2.6) drops out.

explain.text: D's 3.8 is the only mean far from the rest: 3.5 above A and 2.9 above E. Every other gap is 2.6 or less. So 2 of the 15 pairs differ, both with variant D.

items.prose: A market maker splits its EUR/GBP client flow each day into two equal books, and a coin picks the book that runs a new quoting rule. Daily P&L per book has SD $\sigma = 15$, in £ thousand. The two books' P&L on one day correlate at $\rho = 0.6$. The test runs for 120 days.

parts.question: What is the SD of one day's difference, new book minus old, in £ thousand? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the two variances and subtract twice the covariance.

byKey.plus-rho: $\sqrt{720}$ is the SD of the two books' total, where their shared day counts twice. In new minus old it comes off: $2 \times 225 \times 0.4 = 180$.
byKey.no-rho: $15\sqrt2 = 21.2132$ would hold for books with unrelated P&L. At $\rho = 0.6$ the covariance $0.6 \times 225 = 135$ comes off twice.
byKey.no-two: You dropped the 2. Each book brings its own variance $\sigma^2$: $\operatorname{Var}(D) = 2\sigma^2(1 - \rho)$.

explain.text: $\operatorname{Var}(Y_N - Y_O) = 225 + 225 - 2 \times 0.6 \times 225 = 180$. The covariance, 135, is the part of a day's P&L common to both books. So $\operatorname{SD}(D) = \sqrt{180} \approx 13.4164$.

parts.question: Take $\operatorname{SD}(D) = 13.4164$ from part 1 and a two-sided 5% test. What is the smallest true daily gain that 120 days detect with 80% power? Use $z_{0.975} = 1.95996$ and $z_{0.8} = 0.84162$. Give 4 decimal places, in £ thousand.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Solve the paired sample-size rule for the gain instead of the days.

byKey.unpaired: You used $15\sqrt2 = 21.2132$, the SD for two independent books. The design pairs the books, so use 13.4164.
byKey.no-power: 2.4005 is $1.95996 \times 1.224745$, a gain sitting exactly on the rejection line. Add 0.84162 standard errors to clear it four times in five.

explain.text: Here the days are fixed at 120 and the gain is unknown, so solve the paired rule for $\delta$. The mean of 120 differences has standard error $13.4164/\sqrt{120} = 1.22474$. Times $1.95996 + 0.84162 = 2.80158$ that gives about 3.4312 a day.

parts.question: Part 2 gave the mean of 120 differences a planned standard error of $13.4164/\sqrt{120} = 1.22474$. After 120 days the differences have mean 2.9 and SD 14.1, not the planned 13.4164. What is the paired $t$-statistic? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the mean difference by its standard error from the observed SD.

byKey.no-root: $2.9/14.1$ measures the mean against one day's spread. A mean of 120 differences varies $\sqrt{120}$ times less: $14.1/\sqrt{120} = 1.28715$.
byKey.planned-sd: You used the planned SD 13.4164. The test uses the SD the 120 days actually showed, 14.1.

explain.text: Each day gives one difference, new book minus old, so the sample is 120 numbers. Their standard error is $14.1/\sqrt{120} = 1.28715$. So $t = 2.9/1.28715 \approx 2.2530$.

parts.question: Using $t = 2.2530$ on 119 degrees of freedom from part 3, what is the two-sided $p$-value? For 119 degrees of freedom, $P(t_{119} > 2.2530) = 0.01305$. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $2P(t_{119} > 2.2530) \approx 0.0261$. The new rule's gain is significant at 5%.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the upper tail of $t_{119}$ beyond 2.2530 and double it.

byKey.one-sided: 0.0130 is $P(t_{119} > 2.2530)$ alone. A loss of 2.9 a day would have counted as evidence too, so add the other side.
byKey.lower-tail: That is the area below 2.2530. Take the upper tail and double it.

explain.text: Under no gain the paired statistic follows $t_{119}$. Doubling the tail beyond 2.2530 gives about 0.0261. The gain of 2.9 is below the design's 3.4312, yet the test still rejected at 5%.

items.prose: A rates desk trials a new curve model against its old one for 10 days. Each day both price the same bonds, and the day is a win if the new model's pricing error is smaller. With no real difference each day is a win with chance one half, independently of the others. The plan is a one-sided sign test after day 10, which rejects at 9 or more wins.

parts.question: Under no difference, what is the chance of 9 or more wins in 10 days? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the win patterns with 9 or 10 wins and divide by all $2^{10}$.

byKey.exactly-nine: 0.0098 is $10/1024$, exactly 9 wins. The rule also rejects at 10 wins, one more pattern.
byKey.eight-or-more: 0.0547 is the chance of 8 or more wins, $56/1024$. That is above 5%, which is why the plan rejects only at 9.

explain.text: Each of the $2^{10} = 1024$ win patterns has the same chance. Ten of them have 9 wins and one has 10, so the plan's false-alarm rate is $11/1024 \approx 0.0107$.

parts.question: Midway the head of desk adds a look: after day 5 the trial stops, and the new model is declared better, if all five days are wins. Under no difference, what is the chance of that? Give 5 decimal places.

feedback.correct: All five wins is one pattern of $2^5 = 32$, so the chance is $1/32 = 0.03125$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the patterns of five days that are all wins.

byKey.two-sided: 0.0625 also counts five losses. The look stops only for the new model, so one pattern of 32 counts.

explain.text: The first five days have 32 equally likely patterns, and only one is five wins. So the early look raises a false alarm with chance $1/32 = 0.03125$ on its own.

parts.question: Bonferroni's inequality bounds the chance that either look raises a false alarm. Using 0.0107 from part 1 and 0.0313 from part 2, what is that bound? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The chance of either is at most the sum: $0.0107 + 0.0313 = 0.0420$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Bonferroni bounds the chance of either event by the sum of their chances.

byKey.independent: 0.0417 is $1 - (1 - 0.0107)(1 - 0.0313)$, the rule for events with nothing in common. Five wins by day 5 make 9 by day 10 far likelier, so only the sum is safe.
byKey.product: 0.0003 is $0.0107 \times 0.0313$, a product. The bound adds the two chances, because a false alarm needs only one look to reject.

explain.text: Bonferroni's inequality says $P(A \text{ or } B) \le P(A) + P(B)$, whatever the link between the events. Here that is $0.0107 + 0.0313 = 0.0420$. So the two-look plan could run at nearly four times the planned 0.0107.

parts.question: A false alarm needs five early wins, or fewer early wins and then 9 or more in all. Part 3 bounds its chance by 0.0420. What is the exact false-alarm rate of the two-look plan? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Fewer than five early wins and 9 in all needs 4 early wins and then 5 of 5: $5/32 \times 1/32 = 5/1024$. With the early look's $32/1024$ the rate is $37/1024 \approx 0.0361$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the early look's chance to the chance of 4 early wins followed by five more.

byKey.bound: 0.0420 is the bound from part 3, $43/1024$. It counts twice the 6 patterns where both looks reject; take them off once.
byKey.independent: 0.0417 multiplies the chances that each look stays quiet. Days 1 to 5 feed both looks, so that product is not the chance of no alarm. Count the patterns instead: 37 of 1024.
byKey.day-ten: 0.0107 is the plan without the early look. The early look adds false alarms of its own.

explain.text: The early look fires on 32 of the 1024 patterns of ten days. Of the rest, only 4 early wins followed by five more reach 9, another 5 patterns. So the two-look plan raises a false alarm with chance $37/1024 \approx 0.0361$, over three times the planned 0.0107.
